name: Lactantius
status: Church Father. Not counted a saint.

seo.title: Lactantius: his quotes, the riddle of evil and the flat earth
seo.description: Who Lactantius was, in plain words: why faith cannot be forced, Epicurus's riddle of evil, the flat earth, and why he is not counted a saint.

band.lede: A teacher of Latin eloquence who lived through the Great Persecution and wrote that faith cannot be forced.

who: Lactantius was a North African teacher of Latin eloquence. He was teaching at Nicomedia, the emperor's city, when the Great Persecution broke out in 303. He wrote the Divine Institutes, which argue that faith cannot be forced. In old age he tutored Constantine's son. He is a Church Father, but not counted a saint.

lines: The first attempt to set out the whole Christian faith in Latin
Written between 303 and 311, during the Great Persecution

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 250, in **North Africa**. Britannica says 240. He was born a pagan. An inscription found at Cirta, today Constantine in Algeria, has led some to think his family came from there.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: In North Africa. He studied rhetoric under Arnobius, who taught at Sicca Veneria.

facts.label: Taught
facts.text: Latin rhetoric at **Nicomedia**, today İzmit in Turkey. The emperor Diocletian asked for him.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: No one knows when or how. Probably at **Trier**, today in Germany, about 320 to 325. He was very old.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Firmianus**, the name Jerome uses. In full, Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius. Renaissance humanists called him **the Christian Cicero**.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: Church Father. Not counted a saint. No church calendar we checked keeps a day for him.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: No emblem of his own, and no ancient portrait is surely his. A later engraving shows him as an old, bearded scholar at his inkwell.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Jerome lists 12 works, and 5 survive: **the Divine Institutes** in seven books, its **Epitome**, **On the Anger of God**, **On the Workmanship of God** and **On the Deaths of the Persecutors**. The Catholic and Orthodox encyclopedias also count a poem, *The Phoenix*, as his. Jerome does not list it.

traits.title: blunt about other writers
traits.text: He judged the Christian writers before him by their style and their method. He found Tertullian “not sufficiently polished, and very obscure”. He said Cyprian should have answered a pagan with reason, not with Scripture the man thought false. He even repeats a scoffer's joke that changed one letter of Cyprian's name to make “Coprianus”.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 5, chapters 1 and 4

traits.title: plain words over polish
traits.text: He was a famous teacher of eloquence. Yet he said God made Scripture plain on purpose. God “wished those things which are divine to be without adornment, that all might understand the things which He Himself spoke to all.” Of himself he said there was in him “but a slight stream of eloquence”.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 6, chapter 21; On the Workmanship of God, chapter 20

traits.title: wisdom for everyone
traits.text: Cicero said philosophy was not for the crowd. Lactantius, the Christian Cicero, disagreed. If people can be wise at all, he wrote, then “workmen, and country people, and women, and all, in short, who bear the human form, should be taught to be wise”.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 3, chapter 25

traits.title: poor, and still writing
traits.text: He lost his post and his pupils, and lived in real want. Jerome says he “generally lacked even the necessities”. He opened one book by telling a former pupil how troubled he was, “and in the greatest necessities”.

cite.text: Jerome, Chronicle, the year 317; On the Workmanship of God, chapter 1; Catholic Encyclopedia

said.lede: Jerome read him closely. He praised the style and doubted the teaching. Augustine counted him among the Christians who put pagan learning to God's use.

quotes.q: Lactantius has a flow of eloquence worthy of Tully: would that he had been as ready to teach our doctrines as he was to pull down those of others!
quotes.who: Jerome, writing later in the same century. Tully is Cicero.

cite.text: Jerome, Letter 58, to Paulinus

quotes.q: Lactantius, the most eloquent man of his time, educated Crispus in Latin literature

cite.text: Jerome, Chronicle, the year 317

quotes.q: Do we not see with what a quantity of gold and silver and garments Cyprian, that most persuasive teacher and most blessed martyr, was loaded when he came out of Egypt? How much Lactantius brought with him?
quotes.who: Augustine. Israel carried gold out of Egypt, and these Christians carried the best of pagan learning into the Church.

cite.text: On Christian Doctrine, Book 2, chapter 40

moments.title: Called to the emperor's city
moments.text: He studied rhetoric in Africa under Arnobius. Then the emperor Diocletian asked for him as a professor of Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia. He wrote a poem about the journey, now lost. But Nicomedia was a Greek city, and he found few pupils for Latin, so he turned to writing. He probably became a Christian there.

cite.text: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 80; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: The church torn down
moments.text: The day chosen was a pagan feast. At first light, officials forced open the church. They burned the Scriptures and looted the rest. The church stood in view of the palace. Diocletian and Galerius stood “as if on a watch-tower”, arguing about whether to burn it. Diocletian feared the fire would spread, so guards came with axes instead. In a few hours they levelled it. The next day an edict stripped Christians of their rights.

cite.text: On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapters 12 and 13

moments.title: Answering the mockers
moments.text: While the church lay in ruins, two men wrote against the Christians. One was a philosopher who praised plain living but dined better at home than in a palace. He “vomited forth three books against the Christian religion”. The other was a judge who had pushed for the persecution. Their books moved Lactantius to write the Divine Institutes. He also saw the prefect of Bithynia rejoice “as though he had subdued some nation of barbarians” when a Christian who had held out for two years seemed at last to give way.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 5, chapters 2, 4 and 11

moments.title: Constantine's dream
moments.text: He wrote the earliest account of the dream Constantine had before the battle at the Milvian Bridge. Constantine “was directed in a dream to cause the heavenly sign to be delineated on the shields of his soldiers”. He marked their shields with the cipher of Christ, and won. Lactantius addressed his Institutes to him, as “the first of the Roman princes to repudiate errors”. Some manuscripts lack those addresses.

cite.text: On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapter 44; Divine Institutes, Book 1, chapter 1

moments.title: Tutor to the emperor's son
moments.text: Constantine's friendship lifted him out of poverty. Jerome says that in his “extreme old age” he became tutor to Crispus, Constantine's son, in Gaul. Crispus was later put to death by his own father, in 326.

cite.text: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 80; Catholic Encyclopedia

words.note: These are his own words, from his own books, in William Fletcher's translation of 1886.

feature.q: I shall think that I have lived enough, and that I have discharged the duty of a man, if my labour shall have freed some men from errors, and have directed them to the path which leads to heaven.
feature.ctx: The last words of his earliest surviving book, written for a former pupil in the first years of the persecution. In Latin, {la|Satis me vixisse arbitrabor, et officium hominis implesse, si labor meus aliquos homines ab erroribus liberatos, ad iter coeleste direxerit.}

cite.text: On the Workmanship of God, chapter 20

quotes.q: For religion is to be defended, not by putting to death, but by dying; not by cruelty, but by patient endurance; not by guilt, but by good faith.
quotes.who: Against forcing faith, written while Christians were being put to death.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 5, chapter 20

quotes.q: There is no occasion for violence and injury, for religion cannot be imposed by force; the matter must be carried on by words rather than by blows, that the will may be affected.
quotes.who: The same chapter, to the persecutors.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 5, chapter 20

quotes.q: Therefore, with regard to this precept of God, there ought to be no exception at all; but that it is always unlawful to put to death a man, whom God willed to be a sacred animal.
quotes.who: On God's command not to kill. He applies it to war, and to bringing a charge that could end in death.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 6, chapter 20

quotes.q: For if God is not angry with the impious and the unrighteous, it is clear that He does not love the pious and the righteous.
quotes.who: Against those who said God is kind but never angry.

cite.text: On the Anger of God, chapter 5

quotes.q: Nor is there any other cause why we mutually bestow upon each other the name of brethren, except that we believe ourselves to be equal.
quotes.who: On why Christians, rich and poor, slave and free, call one another brothers.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 5, chapter 16

quotes.q: The last and greatest office of piety is the burying of strangers and the poor.
quotes.who: A duty, he says, the philosophers never mentioned.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 6, chapter 12

quotes.q: We can take nothing with us, except a well and innocently spent life.
quotes.who: Near the end of the Divine Institutes.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 7, chapter 27

quotes.q: Therefore it is the Catholic Church alone which retains true worship.
quotes.who: Against the sects of his day, which he names: Phrygians, Novatians, Valentinians, Marcionites and others.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 4, chapter 30

extras.title: Where he is criticised
extras.lede: Later Christians kept reading him, but not without objections. Here are the main ones.

items.title: The Holy Spirit
items.text: Jerome charged that he “altogether denies the subsistence of the Holy Spirit”, above all in his letters to Demetrianus. Those letters are lost, so the charge cannot be checked in his own words. Jerome went on reading him anyway. In the same letter he asks:
items.quote: But who can forbid me to read his Institutes — in which he has written against the Gentiles with much ability — simply because this opinion of his is to be abhorred?

cite.text: Jerome, Letter 84, to Pammachius and Oceanus

items.title: The shape of the earth
items.text: He mocked the idea of people living on the far side of a round earth. Copernicus singled him out in 1543, in the preface of his great book. He called Lactantius a famous writer but little of a mathematician: “{la|Lactantium, celebrem alioqui scriptorem, sed Mathematicum parum}”. He said Lactantius spoke quite childishly about the shape of the earth.
items.quote: Or is there any one so senseless as to believe that there are men whose footsteps are higher than their heads?

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 3, chapter 24; Copernicus, On the Revolutions, preface

items.title: The end of the world
items.text: He expected six thousand years of history, then a thousand-year reign of the just on earth. He thought the end was at most two hundred years off. Jerome lists him with those who held this thousand-year view: “Tertullian also in his work On the hope of the faithful, Victorinus of Petau and Lactantius follow this view.”
items.quote: At the end of the six thousandth year all wickedness must be abolished from the earth, and righteousness reign for a thousand years.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 7, chapters 14 and 25; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 18

items.title: The persecutors' deaths
items.text: He wrote a whole book on how the emperors who persecuted Christians died, and he lingers over the details. Of Galerius's last illness he writes that “the stench was so foul as to pervade not only the palace, but even the whole city”. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes “the manifest bias of the author”. It still calls the book a source “of prime importance” for the persecution. He says he wrote “on the authority of well-informed persons”.
items.quote: Of the end of those men I have thought good to publish a narrative, that all who are afar off, and all who shall arise hereafter, may learn how the Almighty manifested His power and sovereign greatness in rooting out and utterly destroying the enemies of His name.

cite.text: On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapters 1, 33 and 52; Catholic Encyclopedia

items.title: A shallow theologian?
items.text: The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1910 calls him “polished rather than profound”. It says his fine style “cannot hide the author's lack of grasp of Christian principles and his almost utter ignorance of Scripture”. Britannica speaks of his “unprofound view of religion as popular morality”. Yet Jerome kept reading and praising his books, and Augustine named him with honour beside Cyprian.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910); Britannica

myths.claim: The riddle of evil, in Epicurus's own words: “Is He willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is He impotent.”
myths.truth: Those are David Hume's words, from 1779. Lactantius reports the riddle as Epicurus's, in a longer form, so that he can answer it. The closing line often added, asking why we should call Him God, is in neither. His own answer: God could take evils away, but does not, “because He at the same time gives wisdom”.

cite.text: On the Anger of God, chapter 13; David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, Part 10

myths.claim: “Devils so work that things which are not, appear to men as if they were real.”
myths.truth: Not his words, but a later paraphrase of them. The same line, in Latin, heads H. P. Lovecraft's story The Festival (1925), credited to Lactantius. His real line says demons deceive people “so that they do not see those things which exist, and think that they see those things which do not exist”.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 2, chapter 15; Weird Tales, January 1925

myths.claim: “Where is the marvel of the Hanging Gardens of Babylon if we are to allow of a hanging world at the Antipodes?”
myths.truth: The idea is his, but not these words. He does joke that philosophers “make hanging fields, and seas, and cities, and mountains”. But he never names Babylon. Quote sites print a looser version of the whole passage.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 3, chapter 24

myths.claim: Lactantius tells of the cross in the sky, with the words “Conquer by this”.
myths.truth: In Lactantius it is a dream, and Constantine is told to mark “the heavenly sign” on his soldiers' shields. The cross of light in the noon sky comes from Eusebius's later Life of Constantine. Eusebius says the emperor told him so himself, and swore to it.

cite.text: On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapter 44; Eusebius, Life of Constantine, Book 1, chapters 28 and 29

myths.claim: “Memory tempers prosperity, mitigates adversity, controls youth, and delights old age.”
myths.truth: Quote sites print this under his name. We could not find it anywhere in his surviving works.

cite.text: AZ Quotes; his five surviving works

stood.lede: Each line is his own, from William Fletcher's translation of 1886.

circle.name: Arnobius
circle.text: His teacher of rhetoric in Africa. Arnobius also wrote seven books against the pagans.

cite.text: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapters 79 and 80; Letter 70

circle.name: Demetrianus
circle.text: A former pupil, and a rich Christian. Lactantius wrote On the Workmanship of God for him, and two books of letters. Jerome says those letters denied the Holy Spirit.

cite.text: On the Workmanship of God, chapter 1; Jerome, Letter 84

circle.name: Donatus
circle.text: A confessor. Lactantius addressed On the Deaths of the Persecutors to him. Donatus was put on the rack nine times and never gave way.

cite.text: On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapters 1 and 16

circle.name: Diocletian and Galerius
circle.text: Diocletian brought him to Nicomedia. Later the two emperors watched the church there torn down. He tells how each of them died.

cite.text: On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapters 12, 33 and 42

circle.name: Constantine
circle.text: The emperor he addressed the Institutes to. Constantine's friendship lifted him out of poverty and made him tutor to his son.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 1, chapter 1; Catholic Encyclopedia

circle.name: Crispus
circle.text: Constantine's son, whom he taught Latin in Gaul. Constantine had Crispus put to death in 326.

cite.text: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 80; Catholic Encyclopedia

circle.name: Tertullian
circle.text: A fellow African who wrote before him. Lactantius granted he was skilled in every kind of literature, but found his style unpolished and obscure.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 5, chapter 1

circle.name: Cyprian of Carthage
circle.text: Lactantius called him the most renowned of the Christian writers before him. He praised his style, but faulted his way of arguing with pagans.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 5, chapters 1 and 4

circle.name: Jerome
circle.text: He praised Lactantius's eloquence and kept reading his books. He also wished Lactantius had been as good at teaching the faith as at tearing down other beliefs. And he said Lactantius denied the Holy Spirit.

cite.text: Jerome, Letters 58 and 84

circle.name: Augustine of Hippo
circle.text: He named Lactantius among the Christians who carried the best of pagan learning into the Church.

cite.text: On Christian Doctrine, Book 2, chapter 40

death.big: Nobody knows how or when he died.
paras: He was very old by then, and probably still at Trier. The sources date his death about 320 to 325. The Catholic Encyclopedia says it plainly: “when Lactantius died and in what circumstances is not known.”
No last words are recorded, and no later story fills the gap.

saint.big: No. He is counted a Church Father, but not a saint.

churches.note: No day in the OCA calendar
Not in Common Worship or Lesser Feasts and Fasts
Not in the Missouri Synod or ELCA calendars

paras: No calendar we checked keeps a day for him. The Russian Church's Orthodox Encyclopedia calls him an early Christian apologist and gives him no saint's title. In the same article it calls Augustine Blessed and Constantine a saint.

Doubts about his teaching came early. An early list of books, known as the Gelasian Decree, puts his works among the books Catholics should avoid. It names Tertullian, Arnobius and Eusebius's History too. Its date and author are disputed.
Yet Christians never stopped reading him. Britannica calls him “one of the most reprinted of the Latin Church Fathers”. His collected works were the first dated book printed in Italy, in 1465.

tidbits.text: Cicero traced the word religion to a word for gathering things up with care. Lactantius disagreed. It comes from a bond, he said, for we are tied to God by a chain of piety.

cite.text: Divine Institutes, Book 4, chapter 28

tidbits.text: His book on the persecutors keeps the text known as the Edict of Milan. It is the copy posted at Nicomedia in June 313, which let Christians, and everyone else, worship freely.

cite.text: On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapter 48; Britannica
